column2: On the authority of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of my shoulder and said:

“Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a wayfarer.” And Ibn ʿUmar used to say: “When evening comes, do not expect the morning; and when morning comes, do not expect the evening. Take from your health for your illness, and from your life for your death.” Reported by al-Bukhārī.
Bi-mankibī (“my shoulder”): where the upper arm meets the shoulder blade. “As though you were a stranger”: you find no one to be at ease with. “Or a wayfarer”:

one passing along a road heading for his homeland; or [aw] is in the sense of bal (“rather”), by way of moving up from the stranger, who may settle down outside his own land, to the traveller determined to go to his land.

“Do not expect the morning”: with righteous deeds; “and do not expect the evening”: likewise with deeds; rather, act in the evening and the morning. “Take from your health for your illness”: seize the chance to do deeds while healthy. “And from your life for your death”: do in your life what will benefit you after your death.
Giving sincere advice and guiding people to good.
Addressing one person while meaning all, namely the whole nation, to whom this advice is directed.
Urging people to leave this world and renounce it.
Preparing for death and fearing its coming at any hour of the night or day.
Hastening to righteous deeds and seizing one's lifetime before it slips away through death or illness.
Note:
A teacher may alert the learner by placing his hand on one of his limbs, such as the shoulder and the like, so that he takes in what he says.
The noble Prophet ﷺ gives us a great piece of advice: that a person should be in this world like a stranger or a wayfarer who does not wish to settle outside his own land.

The Prophet ﷺ brought this splendid comparison, which spurs and motivates every intelligent believer not to lean on this world, nor to attach himself to it except as much as a traveller or a stranger attaches himself to a land not his own.

On this it has been said: “You hope to remain in an abode that does not remain; have you ever heard of a shade that does not move?” The narrator, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, guides us to the meaning of the hadith: seizing the chance to do righteous deeds while a person is healthy, before illness or incapacity comes between him
and righteous deeds, and while alive, before death comes between him and them. Among what has been said on this:
Prepare for that which must come, / for death is the appointed time of the servants.
Would you be content to be the companion of people / who have provision while you have none?
Another poet:
Nothing accompanies a person, before his death / or after it, except what he used to do.
Indeed, a person is but a guest among his family; / he stays among them a little while, then departs.
Another poet:
Some people's concern is [long] life, but I see / that a long life adds nothing but a burden.
When you are in need of stored treasures, you will find / no treasure like righteous deeds.
